papers.title: ARTICLE: Sovereign Debt Reform and the Best Interest of Creditors
papers.authors: William W. Bratton*, G. Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
This Article is about boilerplate language located at the back of contracts drafted by the world's largest law firms. The clauses in question are process provisions that regulate the amendment of sovereign debt contracts. These paragraphs have been drafted and redrafted by generations of corporate lawyers, yet they have changed little in their broad outlines in more than a century of use. Now they take center stage in the global financial arena, where they govern billions of dollars (and pounds, euros, and yen) of sovereign debt in default and billions more in imminent risk of default. Officials, academics, and even some of the lawyers who drafted the clauses now want the clauses removed because they make defaulted debt difficult to restructure.
How did this arcane preserve of the bond lawyer come to be the cutting edge in the evolution of international financial architecture? Whereas private debt defaults lead to bankruptcy, sovereign debt defaults lead to informal, often lengthy standstills. The creditors can wait out the period of distress, expecting eventual economic recovery to lead to a resumption of payments. But, for the most part, payment resumption requires that creditors come to the negotiating table to rewrite the defaulted debt contracts. Such a "composition" or "restructuring" scales down the sovereign's obligations and causes it to return to health quickly. In theory, this makes both the sovereign and its creditors better off.
There are practical barriers to be overcome before a composition can be concluded. These stem from information asymmetries, from coordination problems, or from complex bargaining dynamics. Sovereign compositions tend to be tripartite negotiations. In addition to the sovereign and the existing creditors, international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) come to the table holding out new loans. In theory, these loans are conditional, requiring the sovereign to reform its economic policies and the unpaid creditors to share the pain by cutting back their claims to induce lending that facilitates economic recovery. In practice, the IMF often acts precipitously, bailing out the sovereign so as to stabilize the international financial system or satisfy some other political goal of its major shareholders. The prospect of a bailout diminishes the creditors' incentive to come to the bargaining table to make concessions.
Assuming bargaining commences, the bond contracts contain boilerplate clauses, called "unanimous action clauses" (or "UACs"), that erect a barrier to success. These clauses, which conditionamendment of the bond contracts' key payment terms on unanimous bondholder consent, govern the majority of sovereign bonds outstanding. A minority of bond contracts contain "collective action clauses" (or "CACs"), which permit across-the-board amendments with a three-quarters majority. Whereas CACs facilitate restructuring of the defaulting sovereign's debt, UACs stand in the way. With thousands of bondholders dispersed around the globe, coordinating a unanimous vote is difficult, if not impossible. Further, a unanimous vote requirement invites free riding: Because the transaction makes the group as a whole better off, an opportunistic bondholder has an incentive to "hold out" - to withhold its essential vote in hopes of procuring a side payment from the transaction's proponents.
The cumulation of frictions has led to calls for the institution of a sovereign bankruptcy regime. This would resemble corporate bankruptcy reorganization, albeit tailored for sovereign debt. The IMF has proposed a minimal bankruptcy architecture, one that would trump UACs and facilitate restructuring in a majority action framework. The United States Treasury agreed on the need for majority action, but has registered a contractarian objection to the IMF's plan for a new statutory scheme: Since UACs lie at the core of the problem and UACs are contract terms, the solution lies in persuading the market to rewrite sovereign bond contracts rather than in overriding them with an international mandate. Now that the official sector refuses to bail out every sovereign in distress, Argentina being the most prominent example, UACs constitute less of a strategic advantage. On the assumption that CACs are otherwise superior to UACs in terms of efficiency, the Treasury projects that sovereign bondholders will willingly exchange their UAC bonds for CAC bonds, ameliorating the coordination problems. Sovereign debt restructuring can then go forward in a framework of free contract.
Sovereign bondholders and sovereign borrowers at first rejected both proposals - the IMF's bankruptcy plan and the Treasury's spontaneous bond exchange suggestion. These real parties in interest preferred the status quo. But their motives were suspect. To the extent that the status quo makes unconditional IMF bailouts more likely, the sovereigns and their lenders have reason to oppose reform, whether mandatory or contractual.Official sector pressurehas since broken the pattern of universal market opposition. A handful of sovereign issuers have successfully departed from market practice and include CACs in new bonds. The present question is whether this development heralds a market-wide shift to CACs as advocated by the Treasury.
This Article inquires into the causes of this multiparty dispute. It takes a new look at the economics of sovereign lending, identifying interests fundamental to the sovereign debtor-creditor relationship that have been obscured in a debate focused largely on opportunism occasioned by IMF bailout lending. This different focus leads us to identify unsound premises on both sides of the dispute between contract and mandate.
The contractarians propound a "free lunch" theory of sovereign lending. They assume that CACs are a first best improvement over UACs, and that a transition to CACs holds out a surplus for all parties to share. Unfortunately, no such twenty-dollar bill has been left lying on the table. In our view, sovereign lenders rationally could prefer UACs to CACs, and could do so even in a world without IMF bailout lending. It follows, on a worst-case scenario, that engrained resistance will prevent a voluntary, market-wide transition to CAC bonds, and that a majority action regime may be achieved only on a mandatory basis. On a best-case scenario, it follows that frictions will impede a market transition from UACs to CACs. If the international financial community wishes the incipient transition to become general and remain stable, it will have to pay for it. Yet it is unclear where the money would come from to pay UAC bondholders to trade their bonds for CAC bonds. In the alternative, the IMF will have to intervene aggressively, forcing model contract terms on sovereign borrowers by threatening penalties for those who borrow with UACs. The best-case scenario, thus characterized, is essentially mandatory intervention.
We accordingly agree with sovereign bankruptcy proponents who doubt that the markets will spontaneously and quickly shift from UACs to CACs once participants realize that bailouts are no longer readily available. But we also suggest that the bondholder community and the sovereign debtors have legitimate reasons for remaining suspicious of bankruptcy proposals. The IMF's proposal rests on a triad of majority action, cost savings, and administrative convenience as it simultaneously attempts to address the need for a better framework for bailout lending and to rationalize the process ofsovereign debt composition. These elements do not import a persuasive normative grounding for a bankruptcy regime. The economics of sovereign lending suggest a stronger, contract-based norm - the best interest of creditors,defined as whatever the unpaid lenders freely approve. Under the norm, only the creditors themselves should determine whether a given composition serves their best interests. It follows that a sovereign bankruptcy process should not attempt to replicate the transactional bias of American corporate reorganization, where the need to close the deal can override other concerns. In the sovereign context, the long-run interests of defaulting sovereigns and their creditors are more closely aligned than those of defaulting private borrowers and creditors. If sovereign creditors do not like the restructuring on offer, it must be allowed to fail.
Under this view, a sovereign bankruptcy regime need do little more than trump UACs with CACs and then leave the parties to renegotiate their contracts. With CACs in place (however imposed), the parties can be remitted to the law governing their contracts - the law of the State of New York in most cases - without needing the assistance of a bankruptcy infrastructure.
But one problem remains with this minimal approach, a problem stemming from the contractual jurisprudence of sovereign debt.Once a renegotiation framework is established, a given creditor's worst enemy may be neither the defaulting sovereign nor the IMF, but another creditor or group of creditors with conflicting interests. The contract law of New York is undeveloped on the question of whether sovereign creditors owe one another meaningful good faith duties. The law of private debtor-creditor relations, meanwhile, rejects the suggestion that creditors should owe duties to one another, leaving the job of constraining opportunistic behavior within the creditor group to the bankruptcy system.Over a century ago, however, in the period antedating the federal statutory reorganization regime, intercreditor duties did exist. As we see it, thematter of intercreditor equity became cabined in the federal bankruptcy reorganization regime after that regime appeared in 1934. Thereafter, state case law on intercreditor equity atrophied, replaced by a regime of contractual self-protection. A viable framework for sovereign restructuring, whether contract based or encapsulated in a bankruptcy regime, needs an adjudicatory authority willing to impose good faith duties across groups of creditors.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part II draws on the economics and practice of sovereign lending to assert that sovereign bankruptcy proposals should not be driven exclusively by the bailout problem. Reform proposals need to address the fundamentals of sovereign debtor-creditor relationships that operate independently of IMF intervention. These fundamentals help to articulate a contract-based norm, the best interest of creditors.
Part III looks at the sovereign bankruptcy movement to show that the best interest norm already has influenced its participants, albeit implicitly. The most prominent proposal, that of the IMF, has evolved towards both minimalism and creditor involvement. Some of what the IMF proposes to provide, however, is either unnecessary or inimical to the creditors' best interests. Most importantly, it is unclear that the IMF's involvement in the administration of such a system adds anything of value to either the sovereigns or their creditors.
Part IV appraises the CAC versus UAC debate. Here we encounter a puzzle: the persistent use for more than a century of UACs in New York-based sovereign debt issues and CACs in London-based debt issues. A frequent explanation of this puzzle centers on the Trust Indenture Act of 1939,which embeds the UAC in publicly issued corporate bond contracts in the United States,therefore implying that a path dependency constrains the drafting of New York sovereign contracts. We reject this contract failure explanation and propose instead a multiple equilibrium explanation. Under this explanation, UACs and CACs are both rational solutions to an intractable problem. The choice between the two entails trade offs, and is a matter of lender preference under uncertainty rather than a function of an efficiency calculation. One factor leading lenders to favor UACs is the lack of a good faith backstop, which results in a need for self-protection. Holding out is the only weapon one has in aworld in which creditors motivated by side deals can impose suboptimal compositions by majority rule.
Part V projects that such side deals and giveaways will occur if sovereign debt compositions are negotiated under CACs. Resolution of these disputes, therefore, requires a robust good faith principle. We draw on the history of corporate reorganization prior to the enactment of section 77B of the Bankruptcy Act of 1934to show that courts have grappled with these questions before, intervening on equitable principles.

matches.theme_name: Do collective-action clauses (CACs), unanimity clauses (UACs), and related contractual devices reliably prevent holdouts and enable orderly sovereign debt restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a nonformal economic analysis of sovereign lending and the historical contrast between New York UACs and London CACs, the analysis argues that CACs ease unanimity and holdout problems but are not unambiguously superior because majority creditors pursuing side deals can force suboptimal compositions absent a good-faith backstop.
matches.generalized_contribution: Majority-amendment clauses reduce minority holdout power but do not reliably ensure orderly restructurings when majority opportunism is unchecked, making unanimity and majority rules rational alternatives under uncertainty.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal economic comparison of UACs and CACs, informed by contract doctrine and pre-1934 reorganization history, to assess holdout control, majority side-deal risks, and the role of intercreditor good faith.

matches.theme_name: Which institutional or doctrinal reforms (statutory sovereign bankruptcy, coordinated creditor fora, harmonized conflict-of-laws rules) are feasible and likely to improve restructuring speed, predictability, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The analysis concludes that voluntary market conversion may stall and that a viable reform should minimally override UACs with CACs, leave renegotiation to governing contract law, and provide adjudication enforcing intercreditor good faith rather than establish a broad IMF-administered bankruptcy system.
matches.generalized_contribution: Effective restructuring reform may require a mandatory change to voting rules and intercreditor good-faith adjudication, while extensive supranational administration can be unnecessary.
matches.research_idea: Evaluate a minimal sovereign restructuring regime through nonformal institutional analysis, New York contract doctrine, and historical intercreditor-equity precedents, comparing mandatory majority voting plus good-faith adjudication with comprehensive supranational bankruptcy administration.

matches.theme_name: What institutional design best balances creditor enforcement rights and debtor-state welfare during sovereign restructurings (e.g., new-money priority, funding of essential services)?
matches.specific_contribution: Applying a contract-based best-interest-of-creditors norm, the analysis argues that creditors should decide whether a sovereign composition proceeds because their long-run interests are comparatively aligned with the sovereign's, subject to good-faith adjudication that restrains opportunism among creditor groups.
matches.generalized_contribution: A restructuring regime can balance debtor and creditor welfare by preserving creditor approval of compositions while policing intra-creditor opportunism rather than imposing a strong institutional bias toward completing every deal.
matches.research_idea: Construct a nonformal normative framework for sovereign restructuring that compares creditor-controlled approval with deal-oriented bankruptcy rules and uses doctrinal and historical analysis to identify good-faith safeguards against intra-creditor opportunism.

matches.theme_name: Would instituting a treaty/statutory Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM) reduce holdout litigation and crisis costs compared with reliance on ad-hoc private mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing the IMF's statutory bankruptcy proposal with the Treasury's contractual approach, the analysis argues that market conversion from UACs to CACs may require mandatory intervention but that a formal regime should do little beyond imposing majority action and enabling good-faith adjudication, because broader IMF administration may add no value.
matches.generalized_contribution: Formal intervention may be needed to overcome resistance to contractual restructuring reform, but an effective sovereign debt mechanism can remain minimal rather than replicate comprehensive corporate bankruptcy administration.
matches.research_idea: Compare a comprehensive statutory SDRM with voluntary contractual reform and a minimal mandatory regime through nonformal institutional analysis, doctrinal study, and historical examination of majority voting and intercreditor equity.

matches.theme_name: How does the composition and heterogeneity of creditors (official vs private, concentrated vs dispersed, activist vs passive) affect bargaining dynamics and distributional outcomes in restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The analysis argues that dispersed creditors create coordination and holdout risks under UACs, while creditor groups with conflicting interests or side deals can use CAC majorities to impose suboptimal compositions, making robust intercreditor good-faith duties necessary.
matches.generalized_contribution: Creditor heterogeneity can generate both minority holdouts and opportunistic majority coalitions, so voting mechanisms require safeguards against conflicts within the creditor body.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal bargaining account of how creditor dispersion, conflicting interests, and side deals affect outcomes under unanimity and majority voting, using contract doctrine and historical intercreditor-equity cases to identify appropriate safeguards.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, disclosure practices, and creditor composition (activist vs passive, domestic vs foreign) affect bargaining, pricing, and restructuring trajectories?
matches.specific_contribution: The introduction identifies information asymmetries as a barrier to sovereign compositions and argues that conflicting creditor interests can redirect bargaining through either opportunistic holdouts under UACs or majority side deals under CACs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries can obstruct negotiated workouts, while heterogeneous creditor incentives can produce either minority holdouts or majority opportunism depending on the applicable voting rule.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal bargaining framework, informed by contract doctrine and historical intercreditor-equity cases, to trace how information asymmetries and conflicting creditor incentives change restructuring paths under unanimity and majority voting.

matches.theme_name: To what degree can contractual amendment mechanisms (exit consents, amendment clauses, consent thresholds) bind non-consenting creditors, and what are the legal and practical limits?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing unanimous-action clauses with three-quarters collective-action clauses, the Article argues that CACs can bind dissenting creditors and overcome holdouts, but their legitimacy and practical effectiveness depend on adjudicable good-faith duties that protect minorities from conflicted creditor majorities and side deals.
matches.generalized_contribution: Majority amendment clauses can overcome unanimity-based holdouts, but binding dissenters requires legal safeguards against opportunistic or conflicted majority action.
matches.research_idea: Use doctrinal analysis, historical restructuring cases, and nonformal institutional theory to determine when majority amendment clauses can bind dissenting creditors without enabling abusive intercreditor coalitions.

matches.theme_name: Which technical design features of amendment/exit-consent clauses (quorum thresholds, aggregation rules, consent solicitation) most effectively deter holdouts while maintaining market confidence?
matches.specific_contribution: A three-quarters CAC threshold facilitates coordination better than unanimity, but UACs may rationally maintain lender confidence by preserving holdout power as self-protection when no robust good-faith backstop prevents majorities influenced by side deals from imposing suboptimal compositions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Lower consent thresholds deter holdouts more effectively than unanimity, but may undermine investor protection unless majority power is constrained by enforceable duties of good faith.
matches.research_idea: Use doctrinal analysis, pre-bankruptcy reorganization history, and nonformal institutional theory to compare unanimity and supermajority consent thresholds under differing levels of protection against majority abuse.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The underdevelopment of New York law on intercreditor good-faith duties creates uncertainty that encourages lenders to retain UACs for self-protection and is likely to generate disputes over side deals and majority-imposed restructurings under CACs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Uncertainty about duties among creditors can distort amendment-clause choices and generate post-default disputes over opportunistic majority conduct.
matches.research_idea: Conduct a doctrinal and historical analysis of intercreditor good-faith law to assess how uncertainty about creditor duties shapes amendment-clause selection and disputes over majority-approved restructurings.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do standardized boilerplate clauses (e.g., pari passu, governing-law, indemnities) generate systemic litigation externalities and market-wide vulnerabilities?
matches.specific_contribution: The century-long use of standardized UAC boilerplate across most sovereign bonds creates market-wide restructuring barriers, yet its persistence is better explained as a rational equilibrium under uncertainty than as path-dependent drafting failure.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized clauses can propagate collective-action vulnerabilities across a market while persisting because participants value their protective features, not merely because of drafting inertia.
matches.research_idea: Develop a doctrinal, historical, and institutional account of how standardized amendment clauses propagate restructuring vulnerabilities and test whether their persistence reflects rational protective preferences rather than path dependence.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: Private ordering is unlikely to produce a spontaneous market-wide transition from UACs to CACs because lenders may rationally resist, but ordinary contract law can govern renegotiation after public intervention installs majority voting and an adjudicatory authority supplies intercreditor good-faith protections.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual governance can replace much of a statutory restructuring apparatus only after public intervention establishes majority rules and adjudication constrains intra-creditor opportunism.
matches.research_idea: Use comparative doctrinal, historical, and institutional analysis to identify when mandatory majority rules and equitable intercreditor duties allow private contracts to resolve cross-border collective-action problems without a full bankruptcy regime.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: Although sovereign compositions can accelerate recovery and benefit debtors and creditors, the Article's economics-based best-interest-of-creditors norm holds that deal-closing efficiency should not override unpaid creditors' freely expressed judgment, so a restructuring they reject must be allowed to fail.
matches.generalized_contribution: The stability and rehabilitation benefits of an orderly restructuring do not justify overriding creditor choice when creditors are positioned to judge whether the proposed composition serves their long-run interests.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal normative and institutional framework comparing the welfare gains from rapid sovereign rehabilitation with the costs of overriding creditor choice, informed by restructuring doctrine and historical reorganization practice.

matches.theme_name: What role do the IMF and other official-sector actors play in shaping restructuring bargaining, creditor incentives, and ultimate debt-relief outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: IMF bailouts can diminish creditors' incentives to bargain and concede, while IMF pressure may be necessary to induce a market-wide CAC transition even though the institution's administration of a sovereign bankruptcy system may add no value and may conflict with creditors' best interests.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector financing can weaken private restructuring incentives, and official coercion may be necessary to change market contracts even when extensive institutional administration is unwarranted.
matches.research_idea: Construct a nonformal institutional analysis of how bailout expectations, conditional financing, and threats against noncompliant borrowing affect creditor concessions, contractual reform, and the appropriate scope of IMF administration.

matches.theme_name: Should courts or legislators prioritize textual formalism or pragmatic crisis-management when resolving disputes implicating sovereign obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on New York doctrine and pre-1934 corporate reorganization history, the Article favors equitable good-faith duties among sovereign creditors over exclusive reliance on contractual self-protection, while cautioning that courts should not invoke deal-closing imperatives to override creditors' freely expressed interests.
matches.generalized_contribution: Courts may appropriately supplement strict contractual enforcement with historically grounded equitable duties against creditor abuse, but crisis-management goals should not displace legitimate creditor choice.
matches.research_idea: Conduct doctrinal and historical research on equitable intercreditor duties to determine how courts can constrain opportunism without using crisis-management concerns to force restructurings over creditor objections.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a conceptual multiple-equilibrium account, doctrinal analysis, and the century-long New York/London clause history, the Article rejects path dependence as the main explanation for UAC persistence and argues that lenders may rationally prefer UACs because CACs trade coordination gains for exposure to majority-approved side deals without a good-faith backstop.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate can persist not because drafting is locked in, but because alternative standard terms represent multiple rational equilibria with different tradeoffs under uncertainty and incomplete legal safeguards.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct the historical and doctrinal evolution of competing amendment clauses and develop a nonformal multiple-equilibrium account to assess whether persistence reflects path dependence or rational lender preferences under uncertainty.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do judicial interpretations of boilerplate contractual language shape market practice and subsequent contract drafting?
matches.specific_contribution: Through analysis of New York contract law and pre-1934 corporate reorganization history, the Article argues that the absence of meaningful intercreditor good-faith duties encourages lenders to retain UAC veto protection and that viable CAC drafting requires an adjudicatory good-faith backstop.
matches.generalized_contribution: When courts do not police intercreditor opportunism, lenders may retain unanimity protections, while majority-amendment clauses may require equitable judicial safeguards to remain viable.
matches.research_idea: Analyze contemporary contract doctrine and historical reorganization cases to determine how the presence or absence of judicially enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties influences the selection of unanimity and majority-amendment clauses.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: In comparing UACs and CACs through conceptual economic analysis, the Article argues that lenders may rationally choose unanimity as self-protection against the risk that creditors influenced by side deals will approve suboptimal restructurings under majority rule.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual veto rights can be rational safeguards against intragroup opportunism and uncertainty when majority governance lacks complementary legal protections.
matches.research_idea: Develop a conceptual and doctrinal account of whether uncertainty about side deals and creditor conflicts causes lenders to prefer unanimity provisions over majority-amendment mechanisms.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article concludes that rational resistance and transition frictions can prevent voluntary market-wide adoption of CACs, making mandatory imposition or forceful IMF conditionality potentially necessary, but argues that intervention should create a minimal, creditor-centered restructuring regime rather than full bankruptcy administration.
matches.generalized_contribution: When rational private preferences preserve standardized terms that obstruct collective restructuring, narrowly tailored mandatory intervention may be necessary, but it should correct coordination and opportunism while preserving creditor choice.
matches.research_idea: Develop a creditor-centered normative and doctrinal framework for determining when persistent unanimity boilerplate justifies mandatory majority-action rules and what minimal good-faith adjudication such intervention requires.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article notes that UACs persisted despite generations of redrafting by elite lawyers and explains this durability through rational lender preferences and multiple equilibria rather than merely through drafting inertia or contract failure.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standard terms may persist despite repeated intermediary involvement because client preferences sustain multiple rational equilibria, not simply because professional templates are inert.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct the drafting history of competing standard clauses and compare intermediary-driven template inertia with a conceptual account based on client preferences and multiple contractual equilibria.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article's multiple-equilibrium account suggests that lenders choosing between UACs and CACs act under uncertainty and may favor unanimity to protect against restructurings influenced by side deals among other creditors.
matches.generalized_contribution: Uncertainty about other creditors' incentives can lead lenders to prefer individual veto rights over majority governance.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal account of how uncertainty about other creditors' incentives and side arrangements affects creditor preferences between unanimity and majority-amendment provisions.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: The withdrawal of routine IMF bailouts may weaken the strategic appeal of unanimous-action clauses, but it will not itself produce a rapid market-wide shift to collective-action clauses because lenders may rationally prefer unanimity and transition frictions require compensation or coercive intervention.
matches.generalized_contribution: Institutional shocks do not necessarily produce efficient contractual change when legacy terms remain rational for market participants and switching entails distributional frictions.
matches.research_idea: Develop a nonformal institutional analysis of whether withdrawing official rescue support changes creditor incentives to replace unanimity requirements with majority-action clauses, accounting for rational preferences, transition costs, and mandatory reform alternatives.

matches.theme_name: To what extent does legal indeterminacy and doctrinal vagueness increase transaction costs and reduce cross-border capital flows?
matches.specific_contribution: The undeveloped New York law of intercreditor good faith leaves collective-action-clause restructurings vulnerable to side deals and disputes, leading lenders to prefer unanimous-action clauses as a means of contractual self-protection.
matches.generalized_contribution: Indeterminate intercreditor duties can distort amendment-clause selection and make collective renegotiation more dispute-prone.
matches.research_idea: Analyze whether indeterminate intercreditor good-faith doctrine raises restructuring frictions and discourages flexible amendment terms through doctrinal analysis of modern cases and historical analysis of pre-bankruptcy reorganization law.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The century-long division between New York unanimous-action boilerplate and London collective-action boilerplate is better explained as multiple rational equilibria allocating holdout and majority power under uncertainty than as drafting path dependence induced by the Trust Indenture Act.
matches.generalized_contribution: Persistent boilerplate terms may reflect competing rational allocations of bargaining power rather than mechanical adherence to drafting defaults.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct the history and governing doctrine of competing amendment-clause forms and develop a nonformal multiple-equilibrium account to evaluate whether their persistence reflects drafting path dependence or rational allocations of bargaining power.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: Although official-sector pressure has induced a few sovereign issuers to depart from established practice, rational preferences for unanimous-action clauses and transition frictions make spontaneous market-wide diffusion of collective-action clauses unlikely without compensation or effectively mandatory term-setting.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual innovations may fail to diffuse despite institutional endorsement when market participants rationally value incumbent terms and face substantial switching frictions.
matches.research_idea: Develop a historically grounded institutional account of how official pressure, established market practice, creditor preferences, and switching frictions affect the cross-jurisdictional diffusion of new boilerplate terms.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE BLACK HOLE PROBLEM IN COMMERCIAL BOILERPLATE
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi, + Mitu Gulati + + and Robert E. Scott + + +
papers.abstract:
A question that courts face whenever they are asked to interpret a standard provision in a commercial contract is how to determine what the parties understood that provision to mean when they contracted. The interpretive goal in contract cases is to recover and then enforce the parties' apparent intentions, as they existed at the time of contracting. This goal implies that courts will attempt to interpret even ambiguous terms in a manner consistent with the ex ante intentions of the contracting parties in so far as a court can recover those intentions from the contract or the surrounding context.But standardized terms in boilerplate contracts between sophisticated parties are vulnerable to misinterpretation. At the limit, a boilerplate term that is reused for decades and without reflection merely because it is part of a standard-form package of terms, can be emptied of any recoverable meaning: this creates a contractual black hole.More commonly, terms that havelost much meaning still may provoke litigation over essentially meaningless variations in the boilerplate language. In this latter case of contractual grey holes,courts may be functionally incapable of devising a plausible meaning that was attached to the linguistic variations at the time the contract was drafted. Thus, regardless of whether a boilerplate term has lost all or only almost all meaning, courts will face an interpretation conundrum that we collectively term the "black hole" problem.
The dilemma that courts sometimes face when interpreting boilerplate is an inherent cost of the reliance on standardized contract terms in commercial contracts. Boilerplate terms are ubiquitous in commercial contracting because they offer the efficiency advantages of standardization. Those advantages include the development of a uniform system of communication that is independent of any particular contractual context.Thus, parties in heterogeneous environments whowish to communicate a shared intent can embody that intent in a fixed and reliable formulation whose meaning does not vary with the nature of the contract or its context.Unfortunately, the very elements of fixed and unchanging meaning that make boilerplate terms attractive are the same elements that can lead to the process of repetition without reflection that contributes to the erosion of that meaning over time.
In addition to the ordinary risks of obsolescence, the repetitious use of boilerplate has two pernicious effects that can undermine the utility of some boilerplate terms. The first effect is "rote usage": some standardized terms may get used by rote so consistently that they lose a shared meaning and become a ritualized legal incantation."Encrustation" is a second cost of too much repetition: the intelligibility of language deteriorates significantly as legal jargon is added to standard formulations, leading to linguistic variations of the same clause.This process further weakens the communicative properties of boilerplate terms, reducing even more their reliability as signals of what the parties really meant.In combination, terms that develop linguistic variations and thereafter are repeated by rote, even after the original meaning has been largely lost, can become contractual black holes.
Contractual black holes present a heightened risk that courts may be persuaded to adopt an interpretation of the term at issue that is antithetical to the functioning of a market that relies on the standard contract to regulate the rights and duties of the participating parties. The market may have disregarded the term before a court gives the black hole a contemporary interpretation. Nonetheless, the market may have an understanding of what the term does not mean, oftenbecause of the high cost to market participants of an aberrant interpretation. Unfortunately, correcting the courts' interpretation in such a case can be a slow and difficult process, even when the judicial error imposes high costs. This resistance to revision is a function of what we will call the "evidentiary vacuum" that results when a term loses its original meaning and lacks an evidentiary record of its contemporary meaning. Here the chance of a court issuing an aberrant interpretation is heightened as compared with a boilerplate term with a well-known meaning.
These conditions appear to describe the case of the pari passu clause, a boilerplate formulation common to sovereign debt contracts for nearly 200 years whose contemporary meaning was hopelessly unclear.The recent history of judicial interpretation of this clause began in Brussels in a case against the Republic of Peru in September 2000, in which a court issued the first interpretation of the clause in at least a half century.The same interpretation of pari passu was affirmed by a federal court in New York in a case against the Republic of Argentina in December 2011,and affirmed again on appeal in that same case in October 2012and August 2013.In each of these cases, the courts endorsed an interpretation of a particular variation of pari passu that required holdout creditors to be paid in full as a condition to the sovereigns paying consenting creditors under a restructuring agreement. Even though this interpretation effectively undermined efforts by sovereigns to restructure their bonds, and even though the courts' interpretation was widely vilified in the market, meaningful revisions to the language of the boilerplate term did not even begin to appear until late 2014.
The extent of rote usage and encrustation in commonly used boilerplate remains an open question because the issue is only nowbeginning to be examined by legal and economic scholars.But preliminary evidence from other markets where standard form contracts are ubiquitous suggests that the pari passu saga is representative of a larger phenomenon, extending beyond sovereign bond contracts to other contexts where boilerplate is commonly used, including insurance and merger and acquisition agreements.To the extent this problem exists more broadly, it argues for a shift in contract doctrine away from the futile and ultimately costly effort to discover a shared meaning that no longer exists.In this Article, we explore whether courts, or other state actors, might better deal with contractual black holes in boilerplate contracts. Our purpose is to begin the scholarly focus on the effects of this phenomenon by using the pari passu story as a prototypical exemplar. We use both qualitative and quantitative data to support the claim that courts searching for shared intent in the case of black holes in standardized contracting can result in substantial social costs.
The Article proceeds as follows. In Part I, we focus on identifying the causes and effects of black holes in standard form commercialboilerplate. We show how both agency and coordination costs peculiar to the inertia that results from black holes can undermine the standard assumption that commercial parties will promptly revise an unanticipated interpretation that generates market inefficiencies. Part II frames the inquiry: Does the celebrated dispute over the meaning of the pari passu clause provide evidence that the current means of revising black holes impose large and uncompensated social costs? In Part III, we evaluate a dataset on pari passu clauses assembled from over 1500 sovereign and quasi-sovereign issuances in the period from June 1, 2011 to May 30, 2016, together with interviews with the participants in the market. Part IV discusses the implications of the finding that, at least in certain markets, commercial actors face extraordinary difficulties in repairing black hole boilerplate following what the market perceives as an aberrant judicial interpretation of the term's contemporary meaning. These difficulties present a collective action problem whose solution can be daunting owing to the combination of coordination and agency costs that may impair the efficiency of standardized commercial contracting in large-scale markets.
