papers.node_id: 100bulrev253!!ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING VENEZUELA'S DEBT CRISIS: HIDDEN HOLDOUTS AND THE PROBLEM OF PRICING COLLECTIVE ACTION CLAUSES
papers.title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING VENEZUELA'S DEBT CRISIS: HIDDEN HOLDOUTS AND THE PROBLEM OF PRICING COLLECTIVE ACTION CLAUSES
papers.authors: Robert E. Scott,* Stephen J. Choi** & Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
Venezuela's political and economic difficulties are familiar and well reported in the popular press.What is less understood, however, is the role that Venezuela's ability to restructure its sovereign debt will ultimately play in the country's capacity to overcome the effects of the current crisis. Venezuela's current inability to restructure its debt derives from several sources, including the current regime's efforts to forestall acceleration of the debt as well as the impact of U.S. sanctions on creditors engaging with the current regime.But if and when the current regime is replaced by a more benign government, the question once again will be at the forefront: Can Venezuela reach agreement with its creditors who claim the right to accelerated payment of over $ 140 billion in defaulted loans? Answering that question requires scholars to better understand the impediments to bargaining that prevent individual creditors of sovereign debtors who hold rights of enforcement upon default from rationally agreeing to accept debt reduction in exchange for the promise of payment.
Understanding the impediments to a future Venezuelan government successfully restructuring its massive sovereign debt requires an appreciation of the differences between individual contract rights and collective contract rights. In the typical bilateral debt contract, breach occurs when the debtor fails to make a scheduled payment or takes some action that makes future payment less likely. After breach, the creditor demands full payment and, in the event that is not forthcoming, seeks a judgment in court.In commercial debt contracts, key terms - such as what events trigger a default, when payments can be accelerated, where one can sue, how one can enforce, and what remedies one can request - are governed by specific contractual provisions. The stronger the enforcement rights granted to the creditor under the contract, the greater the recovery the creditor can expect to obtain in the event of default and, therefore, the lower the interest rate the creditor will demand. Moreover, when a debt obligation is sold to a third-party purchaser, different rights of enforcement will command different prices.All things equal, a debt obligation with stronger rights of enforcement will trade at a higher price than one with weaker rights. We refer to this standard view of the relationship between interest rates, market prices, and contractual enforcement rights as the "bilateral model."
As a theoretical matter, the assumption that different contract rights have varying effects and thus trade at different prices works well in bilateral debtor-creditor-third party purchaser relationships, where the incentives and actions ofeach party are readily predictable. But much of commercial lending occurs through multilateral debt obligations where there are many anonymous and dispersed creditors with different characteristics, each of these creditors having participation interests in a single, standardized debt contract. To the extent that the rights in question operate through collective decision-making among anonymous creditors with different interests, making predictions regarding the future price effects of those contract rights is a difficult task. Any single holder of a bond, for example, may wonder whether sufficient other bondholders will act in concert to meet the required threshold to trigger a collective-action contract term (such as changing payment-related terms for the bond). And the task becomes more difficult when most investors are passive and will not choose to enforce collective contractual rights, requiring the single bondholder to assess whether activist creditors will choose to enforce those rights. This is particularly true when the activist creditors have financial incentives to remain hidden to maximize their returns from accumulating a position in the bond.
Our focus is the standardized sovereign bond contract that is characterized by a single debtor and many thousands of dispersed creditors, each of whom may have different interests and capabilities. In prior work, we analyzed the activities of activist creditors acting in sovereign bond markets as contract arbitrageurs.These activist hedge funds specialize in unearthing and then enforcing contract provisions that the market may not have fully priced, paid attention to, or even understood.The rents that these activist creditors capture are a function of the arbitrage services they perform for the market.But what are the consequences if the market does not absorb the pricing efficiencies that arbitrage services typically provide because the arbitrage is hidden from the market's view? In this Article, we explore the case in which activist creditors are able to capture rents while hiding from the market. Addressing the significance of hidden activist arbitrage for market pricing and debt restructuring allows us to take a further step in understanding in what ways and under what circumstances activist creditors influence the value of collective, as contrasted with individual, contract rights.
We advance a theory of how creditors' contractual rights of enforcement are priced by the sovereign debt market - a theory we call the "collective action" model.We distinguish between those contract rights that a creditor receivesdirectly and individually (a "unilateral right") and those that require collective action among a group of parties to the same contract (a "collective action right"). We posit that markets will price differences in unilateral rights when the participants are sophisticated commercial parties. For example, take the unilateral right to sue under the law of the jurisdiction specified in the contract. If German law is more predictably protective of creditors' contract rights than Italian law, then other things equal, creditors will consider debt contracts written under German law to be more valuable than those written under Italian law and thus will pay more to acquire those debt obligations on the market.
In contrast, where a contractual right requires a group of contracting parties to coordinate in order to invoke the right - such as a term that requires a certain percentage of bondholders to agree to change payment-related terms - the pricing of variations in this collective action term will depend not only on the explicit contractual language but also on the range of investors in the market. A debt contract that by its explicit terms is more difficult for a group of contracting parties to modify (e.g., one requiring a 90% vote of the creditors for a modification as compared to one requiring a 75% vote) may nonetheless have a higher likelihood of modification if the parties to the first contract are more concentrated and willing to act collectively.Collective action requires coordination, and coordination requires sufficient access to information to predict the actions of other creditors. Consider, for example, a party who contemplates purchasing a debt obligation that provides for the right to sue the debtor for nonpayment if a stated percentage of all of the creditors agree to declare the debtor in default. The value of the right to enforce the debt is a function of what those other creditors will do. Estimating that value requires the prospective purchaser of the obligation to determine the probability that the requisite number of creditors will join in the default declaration.
But imagine that predicting what the other creditors will do depends on knowing the intentions of a few activist creditors whose identity is unknown and who may have the incentive to block the default declaration (for example, because they sold credit default swaps on that debt).Now the value of the contract right is highly uncertain and may not be capable of determination until these few creditors reveal themselves to the market. A bond requiring 90% of the creditors to agree may not in fact provide greater protection against a change in payment terms compared with a bond requiring only 75% of the creditors to agree if the market is unaware of the precise positions of the activist creditors with the incentives to assemble a holdout block. In short, where the market is uncertain of the composition and the incentives of the parties to debt obligations with collective action terms, explicit differences among contracts in the rights embodied in their collective action terms may not get priced at all.
To test the predictions of this collective action model against the bilateral model, we collect data on Venezuela's sovereign bond offerings as well as information about the creditors who were holding those bonds. Over the past two decades, more than a dozen empirical studies have examined the pricing of "modification" terms, a key set of contract terms in sovereign bond contracts that set the vote thresholds required for modifying the payment terms of a bond (such as principal amounts, interest rates, and dates when payments are due). Such modification terms are known as "collective action clauses" ("CACs").CAC thresholds generally range from a high of 100% (unanimity) to a low of 75% of the principal amount of the bonds.Achieving the necessary voting threshold is a precondition to the defaulting sovereign's ability to bargain for a reduction in its payment obligations. These restructuring efforts can be thwarted, however, if a sufficient number of bondholders obtain the votes to block a modification and elect instead to pursue litigation to recover the principal amount of the debt. This, of course, is the holdout strategy pursued by the activist creditors who seek to capture rents at the expense of more passive creditors (and the citizens of the defaulting sovereign). Given the greater leverage a blocking position affords an activist creditor, the prediction from the bilateral model is straightforward: the higher the vote threshold required for a modification, the stronger the bargaining position of any given creditor upon default. Therefore, bonds with the 100% vote requirement should command a higher price than those with the 85% requirement, and those in turn should be more valued by creditors than bonds with the 75% threshold.
There are two reasons why, in theory, differences among these provisions - whether a sovereign bond's payment terms require a vote of 100%, 85%, or 75% of the creditors for modification - should affect the price of the bond: First, other things equal, because an 85% vote threshold is harder for the sovereign debtor to obtain than a 75% threshold, the sovereign seeking to restructure its debt is motivated to offer holders of the 85% bond a larger payment to obtain their consent. Second, on the flip side, because it is easier for activist creditors holding the 85% bond to organize collectively to block a sovereign's restructuring attempt, they can more easily hold out and, by litigating, coerce the debtor into offering a potentially greater recovery.
Despite the importance of these CAC thresholds, virtually none of a dozen or so prior studies of price effects among different CAC terms find evidence supporting the prediction that the markets will value bonds with the 100% vote requirement more highly than the 75% bonds. Instead, the majority of studies report the price effect of particular CAC terms to be somewhere between negligible and zero.And for those papers that do find price effects, the direction of the price movement is inconsistent and only for subsets of the data: some studies show small positive effects, others show small negative effects, and yet others find results like U-shaped curves.Even though a holdout strategy (a) requires strong contract rights (so a creditor does not get crammed down involuntarily) and (b) provides returns that are as high or higher than if the creditor is unable to hold out, the empirical research consistently fails to show that bonds with stronger collective action contract terms command higher prices than those with weaker terms. In short, the empirical analysis of sovereign bond contracts has failed to map on to the bilateral model of debt pricing.
We build on these prior empirical studies by using a natural experiment thrown up by the Venezuelan debt crisis of 2014-2019 to test the predictions ofthe collective action model against the bilateral model and other explanations for the absence of price effects. The Venezuelan natural experiment addresses the data infirmities that may explain why prior attempts to test the differences between individual and collective contract rights in the context of these modification terms have failed: most of the empirical papers compared bond covenants issued by different sovereigns, leading to questions such as whether the lack of observed differences in pricing was due to variations not captured in the empirical models across sovereigns rather than variations in CAC modification terms. Looking only at variations in contract terms in bonds issued by Venezuela allows us to control for any differences across sovereigns.
The data support the claim that differences in the terms of Venezuelan bonds that require collective action are not priced when the presence of activist creditors with the reputation, ability, and capacity to hold out and function as a collectivizing agent is unknown. As a backdrop, the research on sovereign restructurings shows that these holdout creditors (usually fewer than 5% of the bondholders) have been a consistent feature of sovereign restructurings over the past two decades and that the activist creditors who have successfully held out have, in many instances, received lucrative recoveries.But lacking knowledge of where these activist creditors are building a position, the market is unable to distinguish among bonds with legally relevant differences in collective rights. In contrast, we find that bond terms that either provide unilateral rights to creditors or for which collective rights are supported by the known presence of a collectivizing agent are priced by the market.
There are normative implications to the market's inability to price variations in the strength of creditors' rights of enforcement until the presence of collectivizing agents is known. While activist holdouts may decrease social welfare to the extent that they block value-increasing restructurings, holdouts also arguably increase social welfare to the extent that the threat of costlyholdout litigation leads sovereigns to adopt budgetary policies ex ante that reduce the likelihood of future default. Absent the threat of holdouts, sovereigns who expect low cost restructuring ex post may succumb to moral hazard and undertake excessive spending. In order to reduce this moral-hazard risk, sovereigns may willingly accept stronger enforcement rights in return for lower upfront interest rates. However, where the market does not price variation in enforcement rights at the time sovereign bonds are issued, the sovereign will not have the incentive to adopt optimally stringent enforcement rights even if, in a world where such rights were priced, the sovereign would be motivated to do so.
The Article proceeds as follows: Part I expands on our collective action theory, discards several of the explanations for the failure of prior studies on CACs to find robust price effects, and discusses an alternative explanation for why the literature has failed to show price effects from different CAC terms. Part II sets out the empirical predictions about differences in the pricing of contract terms that are generated by the bilateral and collective action stories, respectively. In Part III, we report results. Part IV then reports the reactions of investment managers to the evidence of collective action impediments to efficient pricing and restructuring. That evidence raises normative questions about the role of contract arbitrageurs in this and other similar markets.In considering these questions, we conclude that firms that specialize in the close reading of contract provisions in order to enforce contract rights aggressively often are able to capture rents at the expense of more passive investors as well as the citizens of the defaulting sovereign state. This practice also impacts social welfare: the absence of a price mechanism undermines the sovereign's incentives to adopt enforcement rights at the time bonds are issued that optimally balance the ex ante benefits of reducing moral hazard against the ex post costs of rent seeking by holdouts.
I. A Collective Action Theory of Pricing Multilateral Contract Terms
We argue that the reported absence of price effects in CAC terms with different voting thresholds is due to the effects of impediments that prevent the bond market from being fully informed on terms that require collective action. While the value of an individual contract right to a bondholder is relatively easy to estimate, the value of a collective right whose exercise depends on the support of other creditors is more uncertain. And that is especially so if it is difficult to determine whether other creditors have the same incentives to join in the collective exercise of the contract right. Litigation is costly, both in terms of direct litigation costs and in terms of indirect reputational costs for the litigating parties. We posit that many institutional investors who purchase sovereign bonds (termed "passive creditors") will not view pursuing a sovereign in court as a viable option because of both the desire to maintain good relationships with sovereigns and the burden of justifying large front-end litigation costs to their investors. Rather, if no other option is available, passive creditors will simplyaccept the restructuring offer of the sovereign. Another option is available, however, if one or more of several institutional investors who have developed expertise as activist creditors are motivated to hold out from restructuring offers and aggressively litigate their position.Then the passive creditors may free ride on the activists' litigation efforts. In this case, the primary value of the CAC contract rights is the option to pursue a holdout strategy. But that option has value to a passive creditor (who, by definition, is reluctant to reject the restructuring offer of the sovereign) only if it can predict which bond offerings activists will choose.
To illustrate, consider the market pricing of a bond with an 85% CAC as against a bond with a 75% CAC and ask whether a passive creditorwould value the former more than the latter. At first cut, because it is harder for the debtor to squeeze the creditors in the 85% bond than the 75% bond, one would expect passive creditors to feel more protected if they are in the 85% bond, where the greater risk of a holdout will more effectively constrain the sovereign's restructuring efforts. That is the basic reason why the market should rationally reflect the preference of most creditors for the 85% bond, thus causing the price of those bonds to rise relative to the less favorable 75% bond.
But for both the bond with an 85% CAC and the bond with a 75% CAC, the passive creditor must assess whether, in fact, a holdout is likely to materialize. To be sure, holding out is easier in theory with the 85% CAC since an activist creditor need only acquire 15% of the outstanding bonds to achieve a blocking position. But in practice the motivations of the other bondholders are critical to determining whether holding out is plausible. The passive creditor must predict whether there are activist creditors among the bondholders for that bond offering who possess the litigation expertise and capital resources to sustain the front-end costs necessary to resist successfully the sovereign's efforts to restructure. Ordinarily, one might think that the CAC itself would provide the basis for such a prediction. Passive creditors could examine the contract terms in different bonds and predict that the bonds with the strongest holdout rights would be those that the activists would target. From this perspective, the bond with the 85% CAC would be a better bet than the bond with the 75% CAC.
The fly in the buttermilk is that the strategy that generates the highest expected payoff for the activist creditor depends on it remaining hidden from the market until after the restructuring deal is done. Activist creditors are able to extract a larger return from holding out if they wait until the debtor first negotiates a significant haircut with the other creditors and only then litigate against both the debtor and the holders of the restructured bonds until a settlement is achieved. Put differently, holding out works best if the population of holdouts is relatively small so that it is in the financial interest of the debtor to pay the holdouts in full in order to settle with the other creditors at the restructured rate. This means that a holdout creditor has an incentive to hide its plans, including which bonds it plans to target, until after the other creditors have settled their claims with the sovereign. If the passive creditors believe that an activist creditor will purchase a blocking position in the 85% bond because it requires a smaller investment, the activist may choose instead to invest in the 75% bond in order to obtain a larger net recovery. And that hidden information likely will prevent the market price from reflecting the true value of the bond that will be selected for litigation by the holdout creditor. In short, because the activists are hidden, there should be little differentiation in bond prices notwithstanding different CAC terms until the holdout creditors are revealed - which typically does not occur until after the restructuring deal is complete and there is no longer any trading on the market.

matches.theme_name: How does the composition and heterogeneity of creditors (official vs private, concentrated vs dispersed, activist vs passive) affect bargaining dynamics and distributional outcomes in restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a Venezuelan-bond natural experiment and information on bondholders, the Article finds that the practical value of collective enforcement rights turns on whether dispersed passive creditors can identify activist holdouts, whose concealment suppresses price differentiation and permits rent capture at passive investors' and sovereign citizens' expense.
matches.generalized_contribution: In multilateral restructurings, creditor identity, concentration, incentives, and observability shape coordination, holdout leverage, pricing, and the distribution of losses, potentially more than formal voting rights do.
matches.research_idea: Develop a collective-action model and test it with within-sovereign bond and ownership data to measure how dispersed passive ownership versus identifiable activist concentration affects pricing, holdout leverage, and the distribution of restructuring losses.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do secondary-market purchases of distressed sovereign claims facilitate collective workouts versus enabling opportunistic holdouts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using Venezuelan bond and creditor-holdings data, the Article shows that a known activist can function as a collectivizing agent that makes collective rights priceable, but concealed accumulation of a blocking position supports a lucrative holdout strategy and obstructs efficient restructuring.
matches.generalized_contribution: Secondary-market concentration by activist creditors can improve coordination when observable, whereas concealed accumulation can facilitate blocking positions, holdout rents, and restructuring failures.
matches.research_idea: Use a within-sovereign natural experiment and bond-ownership data to test whether observable activist accumulation facilitates creditor coordination while concealed accumulation enables blocking positions, holdout rents, and pricing failures.

matches.theme_name: Do collective-action clauses (CACs), unanimity clauses (UACs), and related contractual devices reliably prevent holdouts and enable orderly sovereign debt restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Exploiting within-Venezuela variation in CAC modification thresholds of 75%, 85%, and 100%, the Article finds that these legally meaningful differences are not priced when activist-creditor positions are unknown, so threshold stringency alone does not reliably predict holdout protection or restructuring capacity.
matches.generalized_contribution: CAC voting thresholds do not reliably prevent holdouts or determine restructuring feasibility when hidden creditor composition and incentives control whether collective rights can actually be exercised.
matches.research_idea: Compare differently worded CACs issued by the same sovereign and combine price data with creditor-ownership information to test whether voting thresholds affect valuation and restructuring capacity only when pivotal activist positions are observable.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, disclosure practices, and creditor composition (activist vs passive, domestic vs foreign) affect bargaining, pricing, and restructuring trajectories?
matches.specific_contribution: Combining Venezuelan bond-offering data with creditor-holdings information, the Article finds that hidden activist identities and incentives prevent markets from pricing differences in collective rights, while unilateral rights and collective rights backed by a known collectivizing agent are priced.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information about creditor composition and incentives is necessary to value rights requiring collective action, and its absence can impair pricing and coordinated restructuring even when contractual terms are clear.
matches.research_idea: Develop and empirically test a collective-action account of sovereign bond pricing by comparing the valuation of unilateral and collective rights under hidden versus observable activist-creditor ownership.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: The collective-action model, tested on Venezuelan bonds, shows that activists' strategic concealment of which issues they target deprives passive investors of the information needed to forecast collective enforcement, eliminating price differentiation until the activists reveal themselves.
matches.generalized_contribution: When exercising a financial right depends on other investors' actions, deliberate concealment by pivotal investors can prevent rational valuation until their positions or intentions become observable.
matches.research_idea: Develop a conceptual model of strategic concealment by pivotal creditors and test it with bond-price and ownership data before and after activist positions become observable.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a natural experiment in Venezuelan bonds and creditor-holdings data, the analysis finds that variations in collective contractual rights are not priced when activist creditors remain hidden but are priced when a known collectivizing agent supports them, showing that private coordination depends on intermediary visibility.
matches.generalized_contribution: Private contractual mechanisms do not reliably solve dispersed-creditor coordination problems when key coordinating actors can conceal their positions, although known collectivizing agents can facilitate market valuation of collective rights.
matches.research_idea: Use a within-sovereign natural experiment combining bond terms, prices, and creditor holdings to test whether standardized contractual mechanisms solve collective-action problems only when coordinating intermediaries are observable.

matches.theme_name: What institutional design best balances creditor enforcement rights and debtor-state welfare during sovereign restructurings (e.g., new-money priority, funding of essential services)?
matches.specific_contribution: The Venezuelan evidence implies that when collective enforcement rights are not priced until coordinating agents become known, sovereigns lack market incentives to choose terms that optimally balance ex ante moral-hazard discipline against ex post holdout rent seeking and harms to citizens.
matches.generalized_contribution: Failure to price enforcement rights can prevent debtors from selecting contractual protections that optimally balance fiscal discipline against restructuring costs and creditor rent seeking.
matches.research_idea: Combine within-sovereign bond-pricing and creditor-holdings data with a welfare framework to estimate how alternative enforcement-right configurations balance ex ante moral-hazard discipline against ex post holdout costs and debtor-state welfare.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: Venezuelan natural-experiment evidence shows that uncertainty about activist-creditor identity and incentives suppresses pricing of CAC differences, while unilateral rights and collective rights backed by a known coordinating agent are priced, weakening issuer incentives to adopt enforcement terms that would constrain fiscal moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries about creditor identities and incentives can prevent markets from pricing collective contractual protections and thereby distort issuers' incentives to adopt terms designed to limit moral hazard.
matches.research_idea: Use bond-level price, contract, and ownership data in a natural-experiment setting to test how uncertainty about creditor identities and incentives affects the pricing and issuer selection of contractual protections intended to constrain moral hazard.

matches.theme_name: Which technical design features of amendment/exit-consent clauses (quorum thresholds, aggregation rules, consent solicitation) most effectively deter holdouts while maintaining market confidence?
matches.specific_contribution: Within Venezuelan bonds, differences among 100%, 85%, and 75% CAC voting thresholds are not priced when activist holdout positions are unknown because creditor composition and coordinating capacity can outweigh the nominal threshold.
matches.generalized_contribution: Formal amendment thresholds alone do not reliably determine a clause's market value or holdout-deterrence capacity when creditor concentration, incentives, and coordinating actors are opaque.
matches.research_idea: Exploit within-sovereign variation in CAC voting thresholds and combine it with bond prices and creditor-holdings data to test how threshold design, holder concentration, and observable activist entry jointly affect holdout risk and market valuation.

matches.theme_name: To what degree can contractual amendment mechanisms (exit consents, amendment clauses, consent thresholds) bind non-consenting creditors, and what are the legal and practical limits?
matches.specific_contribution: The collective-action model and Venezuelan bond evidence indicate that a CAC's practical capacity to bind holdouts is not determined by its nominal voting threshold because concentrated activists can secretly assemble a blocking position and prevent the sovereign from obtaining the required consent.
matches.generalized_contribution: Amendment clauses' capacity to bind nonconsenting creditors depends on actual ownership and coordination patterns, making formal consent thresholds incomplete measures of practical effectiveness.
matches.research_idea: Track creditor holdings, voting outcomes, and bond prices across restructurings to test how hidden blocking stakes limit amendment clauses' ability to bind dissenting creditors at different consent thresholds.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do standardized boilerplate clauses (e.g., pari passu, governing-law, indemnities) generate systemic litigation externalities and market-wide vulnerabilities?
matches.specific_contribution: In standardized sovereign bond markets, hidden activist creditors can exploit collective-action provisions through holdout litigation to capture rents at the expense of passive investors and citizens, while the resulting absence of price differentiation weakens efficient clause design.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized collective-action clauses can create market-wide litigation and welfare vulnerabilities when specialized enforcers conceal their positions and markets consequently fail to price contractual differences.
matches.research_idea: Construct a cross-restructuring dataset of standardized clauses, creditor ownership, litigation, recoveries, and bond prices to test whether hidden activist enforcement produces market-wide pricing failures and transfers costs to passive investors and debtor populations.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: Against the backdrop of Venezuelan bond-pricing evidence, the analysis argues that strong creditor enforcement rights can deter sovereign moral hazard ex ante but enable holdout rents and obstruct value-increasing restructurings ex post, while failures to price those rights prevent sovereigns from choosing an optimal balance.
matches.generalized_contribution: Creditor protections may deter debtor moral hazard but impede efficient restructuring, and market failures in pricing those protections can prevent optimal contract design.
matches.research_idea: Use bond-level issuance, pricing, and creditor-position data to test whether enforcement rights are priced and assess how pricing failures alter the welfare balance between ex ante fiscal discipline and ex post restructuring efficiency.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual drafting (currency clauses, pari passu, waiver language, amendment thresholds) be designed to reliably reduce cross-border enforcement uncertainty and interjurisdictional conflict?
matches.specific_contribution: Using Venezuela's 2014–2019 debt crisis as a natural experiment with bond-offering and creditor-holdings data, the analysis finds that differences in CAC amendment thresholds are not priced while activist creditors remain hidden, whereas collective rights supported by a known coordinating agent are priced.
matches.generalized_contribution: Amendment-threshold drafting alone does not reliably reduce enforcement and restructuring uncertainty because the value of collective rights depends on observable creditor composition and coordination capacity.
matches.research_idea: Develop a collective-action theory and test it through a within-sovereign natural experiment using bond prices, CAC thresholds, and creditor-holdings data to determine whether amendment provisions affect valuation and restructuring leverage when activist positions are hidden.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do choice-of-law and forum-selection clauses determine the enforceability of claims against sovereigns?
matches.specific_contribution: The collective-action model predicts that sophisticated creditors will value a governing-law clause more highly when the selected jurisdiction predictably protects individually exercisable creditor rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Governing-law provisions can affect the value of sovereign claims when they provide predictable protection for individually enforceable remedies.
matches.research_idea: Develop and empirically test a theory of whether governing-law and forum provisions are reflected in sovereign bond prices when they create predictable, individually exercisable enforcement rights.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: Using Venezuelan bond-offering and creditor-holding data, the analysis finds that hidden activist positions can prevent standardized CAC differences from being priced and argues that resulting holdout rents can burden passive investors and citizens and distort sovereigns' choice of enforcement rights, even though holdout threats may deter moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: When hidden actors control the effective exercise of standardized collective rights, private ordering can externalize restructuring costs and distort ex ante clause selection, although aggressive enforcement may also discipline debtor moral hazard.
matches.research_idea: Use a within-sovereign natural experiment linking standardized bond terms, prices, and creditor holdings to test whether hidden activist positions impede pricing and impose restructuring costs on passive investors and citizens while evaluating the ex ante moral-hazard benefits of holdout enforcement.

matches.theme_name: What practical limits do asset-sheltering, jurisdictional immunity, and political constraints impose on extraterritorial enforcement of claims against states?
matches.specific_contribution: The collective-action account explains that many passive sovereign-bond investors do not regard enforcement as viable because upfront litigation and reputational costs make suing a sovereign impractical, leaving enforcement largely to specialized activists with sufficient expertise and capital.
matches.generalized_contribution: High upfront and reputational litigation costs can concentrate practical enforcement of sovereign claims in specialized creditors even when contract rights are formally available to all.
matches.research_idea: Analyze creditor holdings, litigation behavior, and investment-manager evidence to determine whether upfront costs, reputational constraints, and differences in institutional capacity concentrate sovereign-debt enforcement among specialized activist creditors.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a within-Venezuela natural experiment, the analysis finds that standardized CAC voting thresholds are unpriced when activist ownership is unknown and argues that their practical effect on restructuring leverage depends on creditor concentration, incentives, and a known collectivizing agent rather than text alone.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized collective-action terms do not by themselves determine bargaining leverage because their practical effect depends on information about and organization of the parties needed to invoke them.
matches.research_idea: Exploit within-sovereign variation in standardized voting clauses and link bond prices to creditor-holding data to test whether clause thresholds affect pricing and restructuring leverage only when collectivizing actors are observable.

papers.node_id: 84washulrev1627!!F. HODGE O'NEAL CORPORATE AND SECURITIES LAW SYMPOSIUM: PUBLIC SYMBOL IN PRIVATE CONTRACT: A CASE STUDY
papers.title: F. HODGE O'NEAL CORPORATE AND SECURITIES LAW SYMPOSIUM: PUBLIC SYMBOL IN PRIVATE CONTRACT: A CASE STUDY
papers.abstract:
In June 1997 a developing country defied convention. It issued New York law bonds that let 75 percent of the bondholders change key financial terms.Until then, standard form New York law contracts required unanimous consent. But no one seemed to notice the innovation, and just about no one followed suit.
In February 2003 another developing country issued New York law bonds with a 75 percent amendment threshold.This time, the world ofinternational finance erupted in applause and criticism. Major press outlets, finance ministers, and senior executives publicly pondered the shift.Other countries adopted similar provisions under the rubric of "Collective Action Clauses" or "CACs." Academic study of sovereign debt contracts took on new importance. This article is part of an effort to understand what happened and what it means.
Standard - or "boilerplate" - terms in complex financial contracts rarely change.The prevalent theoretical explanation of boilerplate attributes its existence to learning and network effects and associated "switching costs."This body of theory suggests that market participants attach value to contract terms either because they have been used in the past and are well known (learning effects), or are widely used now and/or are expected to be widely used in the future (network effects).As a result, firms might adopt terms that are suboptimal on their own merits just because they are well understood or widely used. Switching may be costly for a single firm because it takes time and effort to produce a new term that works and to educate the target audience about its meaning. There is no guarantee that investors, analysts, and judges will interpret a new term in a way that is favorable to its original proponent or, as the example in our opening paragraphs illustrates, that others will adopt the term in the foreseeable future.
Boilerplate change is poorly understood because it happens rarely, slowly, and quietly. Contract terms do not normally feature on the editorial pages of The Wall Street Journal, The Economist, or The Financial Times, or in dozens of academic studies across law, economics, and political science. Against this background, the dramatic and public shift in sovereign bond documentation beginning in 2003 offers a rare perspective on the contracting process and boilerplate change.
The CAC episode is unusual in another respect. World leaders generally do not know what boilerplate is, much less advocate for it incommuniques reserved for big-picture concerns such as global economic imbalances. Yet for nearly a decade CACs had a guaranteed spot in summit statements alongside financial stability and currency regimes.Moreover, boilerplate theory does not usually contemplate a leading role for the public sector in promoting optimal private contract terms.But in the case of Collective Action Clauses, governments not party to the contracts got credit for driving the shift.Judging from recent policy initiatives, the apparent success of the CAC campaign may have spawned a new model of framing economic policy proposals in terms of private contract reform. The latest public-sector effort to promote GDP-indexed bonds cites the CAC experience as an inspiration, and even adopts some of the organizational features of the earlier initiative, such as the expert contract drafting group.
For all its value as precedent, the public sector's role in the CAC episode remains unexplored. Proponents in the Bush II administration called the shift "market-based" even as market commentary attributed it to government pressure.On the other hand, neither the United States nor any other G-7 government appears to have issued direct threats or bribes - the traditional instruments of "hard power."Financial industry regulators refused to mandate CACs or otherwise promote their inclusion; instead, pressure came in the form of exhortations by economic policy officials.Did the "soft power"of G-7 ideas convince developing countries of the inherent virtues of CACs? No emerging market official would tell us thathe participated in the CAC shift because the clauses could alter the course of a crisis. Even after moving to CACs, borrowers expressed skepticism about the extent of the holdout problem CACs would solve. Alternatively, scholars have suggested that G-7 governments engaged in informational "cueing" to help overcome network effects, a form of "soft" regulation.Here too, no early mover admitted acting in expectation of a market-wide shift; few thought the G-7 capable of delivering such a shift and all worried that their country would pay a penalty for innovating.
A final lingering puzzle of the CAC episode is just how few private or public sector participants in it express strong feelings about the clauses as such. We spoke with dozens of actors whose websites and speeches proclaim the seminal importance of the CAC shift (usually as they claim paternity), yet in our interviews a scant few described the change itself as important in addressing the problems of sovereign debt restructuring or financial crises in the emerging markets. Many were unsure of how the new clauses would work in a crisis; most said they were probably good; none said they were clearly bad. More participants volunteered strong feelings about the process that led to the shift - praising cooperation, grumbling about wasted time and official meddling. Was this another instance of wasted lawyering or runaway process?
If true in part, this description is incomplete and not entirely fair. Most participants suggested that their efforts on CACs had less to do with the clauses' literal purpose (facilitating future contract modification) than with their relative utility in advancing other goals, such as demonstrating commitment to a new crisis management strategy, currying political favor, or establishing reputations in the market. Some were successful in achieving these goals; others failed. Their collaboration produced a revealing study in the uses of contract form and ways of governance.
We depart from earlier quantitative and analytical studies of sovereign debt contractsin favor of an interview-based approach. We have collected over 100 accounts of the CAC shift from market participants,officials, and others who took part in it, and have supplemented these with our own observations from the daily work of law firms and government offices, conferences and negotiations, press accounts, official documents, and of course the debt contracts themselves.
Below we first review the sovereign debt context in the early 2000s, the contract provisions at the center of the study, and the process that led to the shift in 2003. Second, we recount alternative explanations for the shift that have been published to date. We then describe the findings from our interviews and conclude with implications for contract change, the uses of contract, and governance.

matches.theme_name: Do collective-action clauses (CACs), unanimity clauses (UACs), and related contractual devices reliably prevent holdouts and enable orderly sovereign debt restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on more than 100 participant accounts, the study finds that emerging-market officials and other actors were skeptical or uncertain that CACs would materially solve holdout and sovereign-restructuring problems, even after adopting them.
matches.generalized_contribution: Key participants may adopt collective-action mechanisms without confidence that those mechanisms will reliably prevent holdouts or improve restructurings.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct CAC adoption through interviews with sovereign issuers, officials, and market participants, supplemented by contracts and official records, to assess whether adopters expected the clauses to prevent holdouts and facilitate restructurings.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Using interviews, observations, contracts, press accounts, and official documents, the study finds that the 2003 CAC shift overcame boilerplate lock-in even though early movers feared innovation penalties and did not anticipate market-wide diffusion, because public exhortation and participants' political and reputational goals made adoption valuable for reasons beyond the clauses' function.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate lock-in can be overcome when coordinated public involvement and actors' political or reputational incentives make contractual innovation valuable despite switching costs and weak expectations of functional or network benefits.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct a major boilerplate shift using participant interviews, documentary records, and contract texts to test whether network expectations, public-sector exhortation, political incentives, or reputational goals overcame switching costs.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: The interview-based reconstruction qualifies the characterization of CAC reform as purely market-based by showing that nominally private contract change emerged through public-sector exhortation and public-private collaboration, while participants often valued signaling, political favor, or reputation more than the clauses' restructuring function.
matches.generalized_contribution: Nominally private contractual solutions to cross-border coordination problems may depend on public coordination and may serve signaling or reputational objectives more than their stated legal function.
matches.research_idea: Use an interview-based historical case study of a nominally market-based contractual reform to determine how soft public-sector pressure and public-private collaboration affect adoption and whether participants prioritize substantive coordination over signaling and reputational goals.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Interviews and observations indicate that market participants, law firms, officials, and an expert drafting process helped diffuse CAC language while participants' reputational and political incentives often mattered more than strong commitment to the clauses' stated function.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediaries and expert drafting groups can diffuse contractual innovations because participants derive reputational or political benefits from standardization even when they are uncertain about the terms' functional value.
matches.research_idea: Use participant interviews, law-firm observations, drafting records, and contract texts to trace how intermediaries and expert groups diffuse a contractual innovation and distinguish functional motivations from reputational and political incentives.

matches.theme_name: To what degree can contractual amendment mechanisms (exit consents, amendment clauses, consent thresholds) bind non-consenting creditors, and what are the legal and practical limits?
matches.specific_contribution: Using more than 100 participant accounts and contemporaneous documentary sources, the study finds that although 75 percent CACs formally displaced unanimity for changing key financial terms, borrowers and other participants remained skeptical that the clauses would solve holdouts and uncertain how they would operate in a crisis.
matches.generalized_contribution: Supermajority amendment clauses can formally permit alteration of minority creditors' rights without generating confidence that they will overcome holdouts or function effectively in distress.
matches.research_idea: Conduct an interview-based historical case study using contracts, official records, and participant accounts to assess whether supermajority amendment clauses can practically constrain non-consenting creditors and how market actors perceive their limits in a crisis.

matches.theme_name: Which technical design features of amendment/exit-consent clauses (quorum thresholds, aggregation rules, consent solicitation) most effectively deter holdouts while maintaining market confidence?
matches.specific_contribution: Participant interviews and contemporaneous records indicate that the 75 percent amendment threshold spread despite uncertainty about its crisis operation, skepticism about its ability to solve holdouts, and fears that early adopters would incur a market penalty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market adoption of a supermajority amendment threshold does not itself establish that the threshold effectively deters holdouts while preserving investor confidence.
matches.research_idea: Use interviews and contemporaneous contract and market records to examine whether adoption of a particular amendment threshold reflects confidence in its holdout-deterrence benefits or instead results from political coordination despite perceived pricing risks.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The contrast between the unnoticed 1997 innovation and the public 2003 shift, together with interviews showing that early movers feared market penalties, indicates that uncertainty over how investors, analysts, and judges will interpret new boilerplate can reinforce inertia but cannot alone explain when contractual change occurs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Uncertainty about judicial and market interpretation can reinforce boilerplate inertia without fully explaining why standardized terms sometimes change rapidly.
matches.research_idea: Compare failed and successful boilerplate innovations through participant interviews and contemporaneous contractual and official records to test whether perceived judicial and market-interpretation uncertainty predicts first-mover resistance and whether public coordination can override it.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: Through participant interviews, observations, contracts, and official records, the study shows that G-7 officials shifted private sovereign-debt boilerplate through exhortation rather than mandates even though participants often doubted CACs' crisis-management importance and cooperated for political or reputational benefits.
matches.generalized_contribution: Soft public intervention can change standardized private contracts without consensus that the reform remedies the systemic problem invoked to motivate it, because contracting actors may participate for collateral strategic gains.
matches.research_idea: Conduct an interview-based historical case study of a public campaign to reform private boilerplate, examining whether soft official pressure overcomes contractual inertia and whether perceived systemic benefits or collateral political and reputational incentives explain adoption.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, disclosure practices, and creditor composition (activist vs passive, domestic vs foreign) affect bargaining, pricing, and restructuring trajectories?
matches.specific_contribution: Interviews undermine the informational-cueing account of CAC adoption because early movers did not expect a market-wide shift, doubted that G-7 governments could deliver one, and continued to fear a market penalty for innovating.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official signals may fail to resolve expectations or perceived pricing risks when market participants doubt the signaler's capacity to coordinate market-wide adoption.
matches.research_idea: Use participant interviews, contemporaneous official communications, bond terms, and pricing records to examine whether official signaling changes issuer expectations about market-wide clause adoption and the anticipated pricing penalty for contractual innovation.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do soft-law norms, reputation, and market practice substitute for enforceable legal remedies in cross-border finance?
matches.specific_contribution: Using more than 100 participant accounts and contemporaneous materials, the study finds that nonbinding official exhortation influenced CAC adoption through political and reputational incentives rather than mandates, hard-power inducements, or strong belief in the clauses' crisis-management value.
matches.generalized_contribution: Nonbinding official coordination can alter private financial contracts through political and reputational incentives even without formal mandates or confidence in the reform's functional merits.
matches.research_idea: Reconstruct a cross-border contract-reform campaign through participant interviews, official documents, and contemporaneous market materials to assess how nonbinding official pressure and reputational incentives substitute for formal mandates.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: A historical reconstruction based on participant interviews, observations, official documents, press accounts, and debt contracts explains the failed diffusion of the 1997 CAC innovation and the successful 2003 shift through coordinated official-market action and participants' political and reputational goals rather than expectations of network convergence or confidence in the clause itself.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual innovations may diffuse through coordinated official-market networks and actors' collateral political or reputational goals even when isolated precedent, expected network effects, and confidence in the term's functionality are insufficient.
matches.research_idea: Compare an isolated contractual innovation with a later market-wide shift using participant interviews, contract texts, and contemporaneous records to identify how professional networks, official coordination, and reputational objectives determine diffusion.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: Interview accounts indicate that participants adopted or promoted CACs partly to signal commitment to a new crisis-management strategy, curry political favor, and establish market reputations, even though they doubted the clauses' direct restructuring value and feared market penalties for innovation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Financial contract terms may be selected for their signaling and reputational functions rather than their literal operation, while uncertainty about market reactions can constrain innovation.
matches.research_idea: Conduct an interview-based historical process study of when borrowers and intermediaries adopt unfamiliar financial clauses to signal policy commitment or market quality and how anticipated pricing penalties influence that choice.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The persistence of unanimous-consent New York boilerplate after the unnoticed 1997 innovation, followed by rapid adoption of 75-percent CACs after coordinated promotion in 2003, shows that standard-form defaults and the institutions surrounding template change can strongly shape non-price amendment rights independently of clause-specific bargaining preferences.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standard-form defaults and coordinated template changes can shape contractual rights even when market participants have weak preferences about the substantive term.
matches.research_idea: Trace successive versions of a standardized financial contract through contract texts, participant interviews, and contemporaneous records to determine how template defaults and coordinated drafting interventions shape final non-price rights.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The failure of the isolated 1997 innovation to spread and interviewees' fear that innovators would pay a market penalty illustrate how boilerplate's learning and network benefits reduce interpretation costs while switching costs can entrench potentially suboptimal terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardization can reduce interpretation and coordination costs while deterring potentially beneficial customization when individual innovators bear market-education and switching costs.
matches.research_idea: Compare failed isolated innovations with coordinated shifts in standardized contracts using interviews and contemporaneous documents to identify when interpretation, market-education, and anticipated penalty costs prevent bespoke terms from diffusing.

matches.theme_name: What role do the IMF and other official-sector actors play in shaping restructuring bargaining, creditor incentives, and ultimate debt-relief outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The CAC episode shows G-7 economic officials using exhortation and coordinated contract-reform processes rather than regulation, threats, or bribes to promote a clause intended to facilitate future creditor coordination, even as issuers remained skeptical of its restructuring effects.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector actors can reshape the contractual framework for future restructurings through nonbinding coordination even when market participants doubt that the reform will materially improve crisis outcomes.
matches.research_idea: Use participant interviews and contemporaneous official and contractual records to trace how a nonbinding official-sector campaign changes restructuring clauses and whether participants expect those changes to improve creditor coordination.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: Using more than 100 participant accounts and contemporaneous documents and observations, the study finds that few actors considered CAC adoption important to sovereign restructuring or crisis management and that borrowers remained skeptical about how much it would mitigate holdouts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual mechanisms intended to facilitate coordinated restructuring may have uncertain or limited crisis-management benefits in the eyes of the officials and market participants adopting them.
matches.research_idea: Conduct an interview-based historical case study, supplemented by official records and contract documents, to assess whether participants believe collective-action mechanisms materially reduce holdouts and improve orderly restructuring.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: Using participant interviews and documentary and observational evidence, the study finds that many actors were uncertain how new CAC language would operate and cared more about the time-consuming reform process and its political or reputational uses than about its transactional function.
matches.generalized_contribution: Changing boilerplate in complex financial contracts can consume substantial process effort amid uncertainty about new language, while adoption may be driven by political or reputational benefits rather than expected transactional gains.
matches.research_idea: Use interviews, contemporaneous records, and successive contract texts to examine whether uncertainty surrounding new boilerplate increases drafting and negotiation effort and whether nontransactional political or reputational benefits nevertheless motivate adoption.

papers.title: ARTICLE:Exit Consents in Sovereign Bond Exchanges
papers.authors: Lee C. Buchheit*, G. Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
The official sector proponents of the new financial architecture, mainly the G-10 governments and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF), have made it clear that private holders of sovereign bonds should not expect to be bailed out by official sector monies in future sovereign debt workouts.In practical terms, this means that private bondholders will be asked to reduce or to reschedule their claims against a financially distressed sovereign that has sought official sector assistance in the form of multilateral credit facilities or a rescheduling of debts owed to other governments.
The large majority of bondholders can be expected to participate in such reschedulings: They have few good alternatives.But what is to stop a few bondholders from refusing to participate and instead demanding preferential payouts?This question has consumed much of the intellectual energy in thenew financial architecture debate.Some commentators have proposed an international bankruptcy code applicable to sovereign debt workouts that would prevent maverick creditors from delaying, derailing, or exploiting a debt restructuring acceptable to most lenders.Others favor stays on creditor legal actions administered by the IMF as a means of disarming mavericks.The less dramatic have argued for changes in sovereign bond documentation governed by the law of a U.S. jurisdiction that would permit the majority of creditors to make decisions affecting the payment terms of the instrument - changes that would bind all holders, regardless of whether they joined in approving the amendment.
Many of these ideas are regarded by the capital markets as quixotic, the rest as either alarming or truly alarming. All of these proposals are hampered, to a greater or lesser extent, by the need to change existing laws, pass new laws, or alter long-standing documentation practices in order to neutralize the perceived threat posed by holdout creditors. But if such changes erode the confidence of the well-intentioned investors in the efficacy of their legal remedies, the private market may simply withdraw from unsecured lending to emerging market sovereigns.No sovereign borrower wants to hear that it need not worry about the machinations of maverick creditors because it no longer has any creditors. The result is that none of these proposals has come close to being put into practice. Unfortunately, the need for effective sovereign bond workout mechanisms - as the recent experiences of Mexico, South Korea, Russia, Pakistan, Ukraine, and Ecuador illustrate - is immediate.It is possible that given time and additional empirical research, one or more of the above-mentioned proposals will be put into play,but not anytime soon.
This Article discusses a less radical, and more immediately applicable, alternative: using the existing amendment clauses in sovereign bonds to encourage the participation of all bondholders in a sovereign debt restructuring once a supermajority of the bondholders has decided to go along with the deal.

papers.title: AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Empirical Study of Securities Disclosure Practice
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi* and G. Mitu Gulati +
papers.abstract:
How are decisions on what information to disclose and what not to disclose in securities offering documents made? One can imagine lawyers advising their clients on how to comply with the law, especially while facing ambiguous legal mandates. In our imagined scenario, lawyers wrestle with the legal detail in arriving at a reasoned conclusion on whether a particular piece of new information must be disclosed in offering documents. But does our imagined scenario match reality? Is this really how securities lawyers tackle disclosure questions in the course of their transactional practices? This Article looks at how sovereign issuers and their lawyers change their disclosure practices in securities offering documents in response to material changes in the substantive allocation of rights in the underlying sovereign debt contract terms.
One view is that material changes are swiftly and clearly spelled out in new offering documents. Sophisticated attorneys and their clients pay close attention to any change that may affect what the law requires them to disclose and alter their disclosure accordingly. We call this the "Legal Compliance" view. Conversely, disclosure practices may suffer from network effects, leading to "stickiness" in what is disclosed even in the face of material changes in the underlying meaning of the disclosure language. Rather than engage in the costly and uncertain effort of determining whether disclosure isrequired under the federal securities laws, attorneys may look to the market standard disclosure practices as an indicator of the required disclosures. Once a particular disclosure practice becomes standard, deviation from this standard may send a negative signal to the marketplace and, thereby, reduce investor interest in the offering. Issuers and their attorneys may also hesitate to change existing disclosure practices out of a desire to influence how the market and courts interpret the contract. We refer to this as the "Network Stickiness" view. This Article tests between the Legal Compliance and Network Stickiness views of securities disclosure practices.
Focusing on the sovereign debt market cabins our inquiry in a manner that allows us to say something about a specific set of lawyers engaged in a particular type of transactional practice. The sovereign debt market consists of some of the most sophisticated and expensive lawyers in the world, engaged in routine but large transactions (at a minimum, in the hundreds of millions of dollars). It is precisely in the sovereign bond market where we expect issuers and their attorneys to have the expertise and inclination to focus on securities disclosure issues. Contrary to expectation, we provide preliminary evidence in this Article that disclosure practices are sticky even in the face of material changes to the meaning of boilerplate terms.
For our analysis, we examine sovereign bond offerings from 1985 to 2005. We restrict our sample to include a selection of major issuers in terms of deal volume (Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia) and a set of issuers drawn from geographically diverse regions (Italy, China, Philippines, Lebanon, Israel, Jamaica, and South Africa). The sample consists primarily of shelf registration offerings with a limited number of private placements.
Our tests focus on the disclosures sovereign issuers made in prospectus supplements (in the registered offering context) and offering circulars (in the private placement context). We examine the disclosure response of issuers (and their attorneys) for three major shifts in the underlying substance of the sovereign bond contracts governing the bonds issued in the shelf registration offerings. Two of the shifts involve unexpected changes in interpretations of existing contractual language: the "Exit Consent" innovation and the Pari Passu shock. The third shift involved an explicit change in the actual contract language: the move toward collective action clauses (CACs) from unanimity action clauses (UACs) for changes to payment-related terms. This third shift, in contrast to the first two shifts, had beenextensively vetted prior to the shift by market participants, the official sector, and academic researchers.
The difference between the first two shifts, involving changes in the interpretation of existing contract terms, and the third shift, involving a change in the explicit contract term, allows us to examine when issuers and their lawyers are more likely to disclose changes in the underlying substantive allocation of rights in the contract. While all three shifts change the substantive allocation of rights, we hypothesize that issuers and their lawyers are more likely to disclose changes that occur, not through a change in the interpretation of the existing boilerplate language, but rather, through explicit change in the language itself. Because explicit language changes are more obvious, and thus nondisclosure more easily noticed by investors and potential plaintiffs' attorneys, the issuer and its attorneys face greater costs from failure to disclose the contractual changes as part of the offering documentation.Conversely, disclosing a change due to a shift in contractual interpretation may have the negative effect, particularly when the interpretive shift is somewhat uncertain, of solidifying a particular, and from the issuer's perspective, unfavorable interpretation. Alternatively, attorneys pressed for time in a rapidly moving shelf takedown offering may expend only limited resources in searching for possible required disclosures, leading the attorneys to focus disproportionately on obvious, easily observable changes in the substantive contractual rights (for example, an explicit change in the contract language) and too little attention on changes due to external causes, such as an interpretive shock (the "rule of thumb" approach to disclosure).
Part II describes the three major shifts in the underlying substantive allocations of rights that occurred in the sovereign debt market for issuances governed under New York law in the early 2000s. Part III discusses the legal duty under U.S. securities regulations placed on issuers to disclose information on these shifts in the prospectus supplement as part of a shelf registration sale of securities. Part IV sets out our hypotheses and Part V describes the data, countryby country. Part VI matches the hypotheses against the data and Part VII concludes.
