papers.title: ARTICLE: RETHINKING THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE: AN ANALYSIS IN TERMS OF JURISDICTION TO PRESCRIBE.
papers.abstract:
The act of state doctrine requires United States courts to refrain from questioning the validity of acts done by a foreign sovereign within its own territory.This seemingly simple statement has caused hopeless confusion in the courts,has aroused endless scholarly debate,and has provokedvehement criticism from the bar.Recent cases applying the doctrine to foreign sovereign acts affecting intangible property have raised the level of conceptual confusion to new heightsand have triggered yet another flurry of critical commentary.
A basic cause of confusion about the doctrine is that courts and commentators disagree about the nature and scope of the doctrine.For instance, thedoctrine has been called a special rule of choice of law,a doctrine of judicial deference based on the principle of separation of powers,and a doctrine of nonjusticiability similar to the political question doctrine.Critics of the act of state doctrine point out that the existence of these inconsistent theories has confounded the courtsand judicial application of these discordant theories has led to arbitrary and unjust results.According to some critics, the act of state doctrine should be abolished altogether.
This article proposes a new conception of the act of state doctrine.The basic approach of this new conception is that the act of state doctrine should be analyzed in terms of international law principles governing a sovereign state'sjurisdiction to prescribe rules of law.  As used here, jurisdiction to prescribe refers to the appropriate authority of a state "to make its law applicable to the activities, relations, or status of persons, or the interests of persons in things."In analyzing questions of prescriptive jurisdiction,this article employs the useful and important approach set forth by the recently adopted Restatement of Foreign Relations Law of the United States (Revised).
To illustrate this approach, suppose that a forum court is called upon to resolve a dispute involving foreign sovereign acts.  The court determines that under international law the foreign legal system has the appropriate authority to make its law applicable to those acts.In this case, the foreign sovereign has committed acts over which it has proper jurisdiction to prescribe.  The court of the forum state is bound to apply the law of the foreign sovereign to determine the legal consequences of those acts and may not question the results unless they are contrary to international law.On the other hand, suppose that the forum court determines that under international law the legal system of the forum state has the appropriate authority to make its law applicable to the acts in question.  In this case, the foreign sovereign has committed acts over which the forum state has proper jurisdiction to prescribe.The legal status of the acts under the foreign sovereign's own legal system is irrelevant to the adjudication of the dispute by the forum court.Rather, the legal consequences of the acts of the foreign sovereign are determined solely by the laws of the forum state.  Otherwise, the foreign sovereign would, in effect, be amending legal relationships that should be governed by the legal system of the forum state.
Since modern international law contemplates broad and overlapping bases of jurisdiction to prescribe, both the forum and the foreign sovereign will frequently have concurrent bases to exercise prescriptive jurisdiction over the same persons, things, or conduct.In these cases, each sovereign state should evaluate the relevant competing interests by a standard of reasonableness and one state should defer to the other if the other state has a greater interest at stake.
Admittedly, in certain cases, an analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe will be scarcely easier than an analysis based upon a current theory of the act of state doctrine.Nonetheless, this approach can be justified because it offers jurisprudential and legal advantages over the current theories comprising act of state jurisprudence.
, the doctrine of jurisdiction to prescribe incorporates the descendants of positivist concepts of power and absolute territoriality -- the original underpinnings of the act of state doctrine.By building upon contemporary versions of the doctrine's original foundations, an analysis of the act of state doctrine in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe remains faithful to the doctrine's origins and accommodates the needs of the modern international legal and economic order.
, jurisdiction to prescribe is a fundamental and powerful concept that plays an increasingly important role as international business transactions multiply and nations, such as the United States, seek to regulate such transactions across national boundaries.  Developing agreed-upon rules of prescriptive jurisdiction should enhance understanding of the extraterritorial reach of the federal antitrust and securities laws, an area where attempts by the United States to exercise extensive prescriptive jurisdiction has led to international tension and resentment.In addition, the concept of jurisdiction to prescribe has broad explanatory power.  The act of state doctrine and the doctrine of absolute and restrictive sovereign immunity, now considered discrete and independent theories, can be analyzed under this single, unified approach.Also, most of the exceptions to the act of state doctrine can be incorporated directly into the main analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe.The development of a single and comprehensive theory, applicable to areas now considered governed by independent legal doctrines and exceptions, offers the advantages of economy and simplicity.
, the doctrine of jurisdiction to prescribe is governed by rules of international law, now recognized as part of the federal law of the United States.According to legal scholars, the act of state doctrine "is probably the single most important reason for the arrested development of international law in the United States."A theory of the act of state doctrine basedupon jurisdiction to prescribe will allow United States courts to contribute to the development of international law.Moreover, the proposed new conception of the act of state doctrine satisfies the judicial concern that the doctrine should be governed by federal law, a concern that has profoundly influenced the doctrine's previous development.
, an act of state analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe will bring much needed analytical clarity to current act of state disputes involving intangible property and contract rights.  Since traditional act of state analysis offers little guidance in this area, courts and commentators propose conflicting and confusing new approaches to the application of the act of state doctrine to sovereign defaults on private loans and sovereign expropriations of foreign bank branches or deposits.Moreover, given the likelihood of increasing numbers of international business transactions involving intangible property and contract rights, it will prove useful to invest scholarly and judicial energy into developing principles regulating the competence of nations to prescribe rules of law governing intangible property.
Part I of this article sets forth a history and development of theories of the act of state doctrine.  This section traces the major shifts in the jurisprudential and legal foundations of the doctrine that occurred between its birth in the nineteenth century and its reemergence in the latter half of the twentieth century.  These shifts contributed to the development of incompatible theories of the doctrine.  Part II demonstrates that each of these current theories is seriously flawed for various jurisprudential, legal, and practical reasons.  Part III first proposes and defends an analysis of the act of state doctrine in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe, and argues that the proposed new conception of the doctrine will serve a valuable and unique function in the modern international legal order.  Part III then applies an act of state analysis in terms of jurisdiction to prescribe to major act of state cases and to recent cases involving intangible property.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE IN CONTRACT CASES AS A CONFLICT-OF-LAWS RULE 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.abstract:
Courts have recently begun to apply the act of state doctrine in cases in which a foreign obligor claims that a foreign act of state modifies the contractual obligation owed to a U.S. obligee.Allied Bank International v. Banco Credito Agricola de Cartagois the best known case in this category. For some time courts have encountered a second category of cases involving the performance of contracts.  In these cases a party claims that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation of a U.S. obligor owed to a foreign obligee.Alfred Dunhill of London, Inc. v. Republic of Cubamay serve as an example.  In some of these performance of contract cases the courts have held that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation; in others, courts have held to the contrary. In all these cases the central question was whether a commercial agreement that had contacts with both the United States and the foreign country was affected by a foreign law or decree promulgated after the contract had been entered into.
Professor Henkin has said that the act of state doctrine is a conflict-of-laws rule.This statement is undoubtedly correct because a rule dealing with the question whether a foreign law or the law of the forum applies to an agreement is a question of conflict of laws.Professor Henkin's statement has been repeated many times by courtsand commentators.Courts and commentators, however, have not analyzed the statement's meaning in connection with contract cases.  The question in these cases is whether and to what extent the act of state doctrine modifies the traditional conflict-of-laws rules applicable to contracts.
This article compares the results that courts have reached by applying or rejecting the act of state doctrine in cases involving performance of contract disputes with the results they would have reached by applying the traditional conflict-of-laws approaches.  The article demonstrates that the results reached in such cases under the act of state doctrine could also have been reached by applying traditional conflict-of-laws rules.  Consequently, the act of state doctrine as applied to contract cases is nothing but a new and fancy dress for old solutions.
